title: Meaning, Reference, and Sense
description: What words mean — and the gap between word and world

concepts.title: Sense and Reference — Frege's Distinction
concepts.contentHtml:
The philosopher Gottlob Frege distinguished two aspects of meaning:

Reference (Bedeutung): the thing in the world a word picks out. 'The morning star' and 'the evening star' both refer to Venus — same referent.

Sense (Sinn): the way a word picks out its referent — its descriptive content. 'Morning star' (star visible in the morning) and 'evening star' (star visible at night) have different senses, even though they refer to the same planet.

This explains why 'the morning star is the evening star' is informative (different senses), while 'the morning star is the morning star' is trivial. Meaning is not just reference.

concepts.title: Lexical Relations — Synonymy, Antonymy, Hyponymy
concepts.contentHtml:
Words relate to other words in systematic semantic ways:

  • Synonymy: same (or near-same) meaning — couch / sofa, happy / joyful. Perfect synonymy is rare; words usually differ in register or connotation.
  • Antonymy: opposite meaning — hot / cold (gradable), dead / alive (complementary, no middle ground).
  • Hyponymy: one word's meaning is included in another's. Rose is a hyponym of flower; flower is the hypernym. Knowing 'it is a rose' entails 'it is a flower'.

These relations structure the mental lexicon and underlie semantic inference. The semantic web of a language shapes what contrasts are easy to express.

concepts.title: Prototype Theory and Fuzzy Categories
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical semantics defines categories by necessary and sufficient features: something is a bachelor if and only if it is adult + male + unmarried. But Eleanor Rosch (1970s) showed that real categories have prototypes — best examples — and fuzzy edges.

Is a penguin a bird? Technically yes, but it's a poor prototype (can't fly, lives in water). A robin is a better prototype. People judge robins as 'more bird-like' than penguins — faster, more reliable responses in experiments.

The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (linguistic relativity) asks whether the category words a language provides shape cognition. Russian has separate words for light blue (goluboy) and dark blue (siniy) — Russian speakers discriminate blues faster at the boundary than English speakers. Language subtly shapes thought.

title: Entailment, Presupposition, and Ambiguity
description: The logic of meaning — what sentences imply and assume

concepts.title: Entailment
concepts.contentHtml:
Entailment is the logically necessary meaning relationship between sentences: sentence A entails B if whenever A is true, B must also be true.

'She killed the spider' entails 'The spider died' — you cannot kill without causing death. 'I ate the cake' entails 'The cake existed'. 'John is a bachelor' entails 'John is unmarried'.

Entailment is one-directional: 'The spider died' does not entail 'She killed it' (the spider might have died of old age). Mutual entailment (A entails B and B entails A) produces synonymy. Entailments are part of a word's meaning — testing them is a key tool in semantic analysis.

concepts.title: Presupposition
concepts.contentHtml:
Presupposition is a background assumption that a sentence takes for granted — a precondition for the sentence's being meaningful rather than true or false.

'The King of France is bald' presupposes there is a King of France. If there isn't, then on Strawson's influential view (1950) the sentence isn't false but lacks a truth value; Russell (1905) had argued it is simply false. Presuppositions survive negation: 'The King of France is NOT bald' still presupposes the King exists.

Russell's famous puzzle about 'the present King of France' (a definite description without a referent) inspired a century of philosophical and linguistic debate about presupposition vs assertion. Presupposition is exploited in loaded questions: 'Have you stopped cheating?' presupposes you were cheating.

concepts.title: Lexical and Structural Ambiguity
concepts.contentHtml:
Lexical ambiguity: a single word has multiple senses. 'bank' (river bank vs financial institution). 'Bark' (tree bark vs dog sound). Context usually resolves this, but jokes exploit the ambiguity deliberately.

Structural ambiguity: the sentence's syntactic structure is ambiguous. 'Visiting relatives can be boring' — are visiting relatives the ones visiting, or are you visiting them? The scope of quantifiers creates structural ambiguity: 'Every student read a book' — one book (wide scope) or different books (narrow scope)?

Scope ambiguity is especially important in formal semantics: 'Every linguist loves some philosopher' — is there one philosopher loved by all, or a different one for each linguist? Truth conditions differ.

title: Grice and Conversational Implicature
description: How we communicate far more than we literally say

concepts.title: The Cooperative Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
Paul Grice (1975) proposed that conversation is rational cooperation. Speakers follow a Cooperative Principle: make your contribution appropriate to the exchange's current purpose. This principle generates four maxims:

  • Quantity: be as informative as required (not more, not less)
  • Quality: be truthful; don't say what you believe false
  • Relation: be relevant
  • Manner: be clear, brief, orderly; avoid ambiguity and obscurity

Violations or apparent violations of these maxims trigger implicatures — inferences the hearer draws to preserve the assumption of cooperation.

concepts.title: Conversational Implicature
concepts.contentHtml:
A conversational implicature is a meaning inferred from the context of an utterance, not its literal content. Hearers assume cooperation and reason backward to what the speaker must have meant.

A: 'Can you pass the salt?'
B: 'Yes.' (passes nothing) — technically answers, but violates cooperative expectations. The normal implicature is a request, and hearers treat it as one.

'Some students passed.' Quantity implicature: if all had passed, a cooperative speaker would have said 'all'. Saying 'some' implicates 'not all'. But this is cancellable: 'Some, in fact all, passed' — unlike entailments, implicatures can be withdrawn.

concepts.title: Speech Acts — Austin and Searle
concepts.contentHtml:
J.L. Austin's How to Do Things with Words (1962) showed that utterances don't just describe — they perform actions. Speech act theory distinguishes:

  • Locutionary act: the literal saying
  • Illocutionary act: what you're doing — promising, warning, requesting, declaring
  • Perlocutionary act: the effect on the hearer

Searle categorized illocutionary acts: assertives (claims), directives (requests), commissives (promises), expressives (thanks, apologies), declaratives ('I now pronounce you...', which changes the world by being uttered).

Indirect speech acts: 'It's cold in here' (assertive on the surface) performs a directive (close the window, please) in context.

title: Deixis, Reference Tracking, and Discourse
description: How meaning anchors to context — and connects across sentences

concepts.title: Deixis — Context-Dependent Reference
concepts.contentHtml:
Deixis (from Greek 'pointing') is the linguistic encoding of context-dependent reference. Deictic expressions only have meaning relative to a speech situation.

  • Person deixis: I, you, we — who is speaking, who is addressed
  • Spatial deixis: here, there, this, that — location relative to speaker
  • Temporal deixis: now, then, yesterday, tomorrow — time relative to utterance

Languages differ in how finely they distinguish deixis. English 'this/that' marks proximal vs distal. Japanese has a three-way distinction: kore (near speaker), sore (near addressee), are (far from both). Some languages distinguish four or more degrees of distance. Deixis is universal — all languages have it — but its granularity varies.

concepts.title: Anaphora and Reference Tracking in Discourse
concepts.contentHtml:
Discourse — connected text or talk — requires tracking referents across sentences. Anaphora is the use of a word to refer back to an earlier expression: 'John came in. He sat down.' — 'he' refers back to John.

Cataphora is the reverse: referring forward. 'Before he sat down, John came in.' — 'he' anticipates John.

Languages differ in how they track reference. Some use null pronouns (pro-drop): Spanish habla ('(he/she) speaks') with no overt subject. Chinese can omit topic-tracked subjects for many clauses. Many Native American languages have elaborate evidential and reference-tracking systems to keep multiple discourse referents clear across long narratives.

concepts.title: Metaphor and Conceptual Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
Lakoff and Johnson's Metaphors We Live By (1980) argued that metaphor is not literary decoration but a fundamental structure of human thought. We understand abstract domains by mapping them onto concrete ones.

ARGUMENT IS WAR: 'Your claim is indefensible.' 'He attacked every weak point.' 'I demolished his argument.' — We talk about arguments using military vocabulary because we conceptualize them that way.

TIME IS MONEY: 'Don't waste my time.' 'I've invested a lot of time in this.' 'How do you spend your evenings?' Cross-linguistic research shows that while conceptual metaphors are widespread, they're not universal — culture shapes which mappings are conventional.

title: Formal Semantics and Compositionality
description: Truth conditions, logical form, and how sentence meaning builds from parts

concepts.title: Truth-Conditional Semantics
concepts.contentHtml:
Truth-conditional semantics holds that knowing the meaning of a sentence is knowing the conditions under which it is true. 'Snow is white' is true iff snow is white.

This approach, rooted in Frege, Russell, and Tarski, treats sentence meanings as propositions — abstract objects that have truth values. It allows formal analysis: sentences are translated into logical forms (predicate calculus), then evaluated against a model.

'Every student passed' → ∀x (student(x) → passed(x)). This notation makes entailment relations explicit and calculable. Formal semantics connects linguistics to logic and computer science, and shaped early natural language processing.

concepts.title: Compositionality — Frege's Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
Frege's principle of compositionality: the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and how they are combined (the syntax).

'The dog ate the fish' — we compute the sentence's meaning by combining the meanings of each word according to the syntactic structure. We have never heard this exact sentence before, yet we understand it immediately — because meaning is compositional.

Compositionality explains linguistic creativity. We can understand arbitrarily novel sentences. It also creates challenges: idioms ('kick the bucket' = die) are not compositional. Metaphors strain compositionality. Quotation and intensional contexts ('John believes Santa is real') block simple composition because reference behaves differently inside belief reports.

concepts.title: Tense, Aspect, and Modality
concepts.contentHtml:
Sentences encode time and possibility through tense, aspect, and modality — each a rich semantic domain.

Tense locates events in time relative to the utterance. Not all languages grammaticalize tense — Mandarin uses adverbs; Hopi (controversially) was claimed to lack tense altogether.

Aspect encodes the internal structure of events: progressive (ongoing), perfective (completed). Russian has perfective/imperfective as a core distinction: pisal (was writing, imperfective) vs napisal (wrote/finished writing, perfective).

Modality: epistemic ('She must be tired' — I infer), deontic ('She must go' — obligation). Languages grammaticalize these differently, but all languages express modality in some form.
